Juveniles of the White-browed crake emerge from eggs weighing just 7.3 grams [Ww0 = 7.3 grams], a remarkably modest initial body mass that underscores the altricial nature of the newly hatched chick. The developmental timeline is tightly linked to incubation conditions; at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the embryo completes its development and the chick hatches after approximately 18 days [ab = approximately 18 days]. This relatively short incubation period is consistent with those reported for other small-bodied rallids, particularly species that breed in tropical and subtropical marshlands where nest predation risk is elevated. Following hatching, the altricial nestling remains entirely dependent on biparental provisioning, undergoing rapid somatic growth over the subsequent weeks. The nestling feather-growing stage culminates in the achievement of sustained flight, with fledging occurring 60 days after hatching [tx = 60 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This protracted nestling period, lasting two full months, is comparatively long for a rail of this size and may reflect the energetic demands of flight feather maturation in a wetland environment where aquatic locomotion also must be learned. The downy chick, initially brooded closely by both parents, gradually transitions to a semi-precocial phase as pin feathers emerge.

The same individuals may produce between 1 and 2 clutches annually [F_R_i = between 1 and 2 clutches annually], depending on local food availability and the duration of the wet season. In the field, nesting territories are aggressively defended by both parents, who share incubation duties equally. The calcareous eggs themselves are cryptically colored, reducing detection by avian and mammalian predators. Reproductive output is further influenced by adult body condition; females in better physical state are more likely to initiate a second clutch within a single breeding season. When environmental conditions are favorable, the annual fecundity can approach eight offspring per breeding pair, though average values are typically lower.

The oldest documented individuals are typically those that have successfully navigated the challenges of seasonal habitat desiccation and fluctuating food resources. This extended lifespan carries implications for population dynamics, as experienced adults contribute disproportionately to recruitment over many breeding seasons. It also permits a relatively slow pace of life, with deferred reproduction and extended parental care being key features of the species' demography. Comparative data from congeneric species in more seasonal environments suggest that lifespan may be modulated by latitude, with tropical populations potentially living longer than temperate ones.

Female body mass in the species can range from 40 to 62.5 grams, with the upper end of this range typically achieved by individuals in prime breeding condition. The relatively modest metabolic expenditure suggests an energy-saving strategy consistent with the crake's sedentary, marsh-dwelling existence. Indeed, active foraging for aquatic invertebrates and plant matter in shallow water likely requires only moderate daily energetic costs. This low maintenance metabolism also allows the species to persist on relatively sparse food resources during dry-season bottlenecks. In comparison to other members of the Rallidae, the White-browed crake's metabolic rate aligns closely with that of the similarly sized Baillon's crake, though it is somewhat lower than that of more active, open-water foragers like the Common moorhen.
